supportingExcerpt: Epithelium forms linings, coverings and glands; an epithelial cell is not necessarily malignant. A basement membrane is extracellular supporting material beneath an epithelium, distinct from each cell’s lipid membrane. Stroma includes supporting cells, extracellular matrix and vascular structures, rather than only collagen or fibroblasts. Immune cells and other nonmalignant cells can contribute to a tumor specimen. The relevant compartments depend on the tissue and disease.

Bulk RNA or protein measurements combine contributions from sampled cells. A stronger signal can reflect more cells of one type, changed expression within cells, or both. Spatial review and suitable cell markers help test attribution; a mixed-tissue result should not automatically be assigned to cancer cells. Normal and cancer breast atlases provide defined examples of this cellular diversity.

An epithelial marker helps identify a cell compartment; a positive lineage stain alone does not establish malignancy or invasion. Tissue architecture matters. For an epithelial carcinoma, assessing in-situ versus invasive disease includes microscopic review of the basement membrane and surrounding tissue. The SEER summary-stage manual retains site-specific exceptions; this boundary is not a universal staging rule for every cancer.

Inherited germline variants came through an egg or sperm and are generally present across many tissues. A de novo constitutional variant need not have been inherited from a parent. Changes arising after fertilization can create mosaic distributions. Somatic variants occur in body-cell lineages, including normal tissues as well as cancers. Origin, distribution, harmfulness and transmissibility are separate questions; neither a variant class nor a large read fraction settles them.

Suitable tumor/normal comparison can help attribute origin, but blood can carry acquired hematopoietic clones. Plasma variants can arise from those clones as well as a tumor. Mosaicism, contamination, specimen suitability and assay limits require assessment rather than automatic subtraction of every blood-matching variant.

In two invented histories, an early constitutional variant may be inherited or de novo, whereas a later variant can mark a mosaic body-cell lineage, including a normal blood clone. A partial set of sampled cells leaves reproductive-cell involvement and unsampled tumour-cell genotypes unknown. Suppose a cartoon contains two marked blood cells among four and four marked DNA fragments among eight. Those are counts of chosen symbols, not measured allele fractions, a tumour fraction or evidence of inheritance. Plasma fragments are not intact circulating cells, and arrows from blood cells or tumour cells describe possible DNA contributions, not an exhaustive source map or proof of a particular fragment's origin.

Amino acids join through peptide bonds into polypeptide chains; linked amino acids are residues. Peptide and protein usage overlaps without a universal length boundary. A protein may contain one or several chains, folded domains and flexible regions. Processing, chemical modifications, localization, production and degradation affect its form and behavior. Genes specify coding templates, but a DNA or RNA finding does not measure the resulting protein’s intact structure or activity.

An antibody may recognize an epitope on more than one product form or a remaining fragment. Many mass-spectrometry workflows digest proteins into peptides: a shared detected peptide cannot distinguish every full-length form. A candidate peptide sequence also does not establish its display by HLA. Separate assays address amount, location, intact form, function and antigen presentation.

In an invented comparison, two related protein forms R1 and R2 both contain the same short amino-acid sequence, but R2 lacks a region present in R1. Detecting that shared peptide after digestion does not distinguish the intact forms or prove their activity. Folding changes the chain's arrangement in space without changing its residue order; cutting off a terminal segment is a different processing example and is not required for every protein. Neither a sequence that could yield a peptide nor its measurement in a digest establishes display by HLA.

Primary structure describes sequence; secondary structure describes local arrangements; tertiary structure describes a chain’s organization; quaternary structure describes assembly between chains. These are levels of description, rather than four obligatory stages. A domain is a recognizable structural unit; a motif is a recurring sequence or structural pattern. An interface is a contact surface and can combine residues far apart in sequence. Intrinsically disordered regions can have normal functions without one stable isolated fold.

Experimental structures reflect particular preparations and conditions, and may omit flexible regions. In AlphaFold2, pLDDT concerns local structural confidence, while predicted aligned error helps assess uncertainty in relative region placement. A confident domain cannot certify a proposed inter-domain pocket or contact. Neither score measures binding affinity, protein abundance, a variant’s functional effect or clinical benefit.

Consider one invented chain with two domains joined by one linker. Two candidate arrangements can preserve both local folds yet create different gaps between the domains. A proposed interdomain pocket belongs to that joint geometry; a confident domain alone does not establish it. Alternative pictures do not demonstrate molecular motion or disorder. The cartoon supplies neither measured coordinates nor ligand binding, affinity or activity.

DNA contains nucleotide chains with a sugar–phosphate backbone and the bases A, T, C and G. Complementary A–T and C–G pairing joins antiparallel strands. Nuclear chromosomes contain DNA associated with proteins as chromatin; nucleosomes organize DNA around histones. Mitochondria carry a separate genome. A gene is a functional region within DNA, rather than an entire chromosome. Replication copies DNA, while transcription produces RNA from a selected template. Packaging and gene presence do not establish active transcription or a functional protein.

For a short invented duplex, 5-prime ATCG 3-prime pairs with 3-prime TAGC 5-prime. The paired bases sit between sugar-phosphate backbones, and nuclear DNA can wrap around histone cores to form nucleosomes. A gene occupies a region of DNA, not the entire chromosome. A packaging cartoon does not establish one universal 30 nm fibre, an X-shaped chromosome at every stage, copy number or gene activity.

A protein-coding gene supplies RNA that can be translated into a polypeptide, while a noncoding RNA gene produces a functional RNA. Promoters and other regulatory regions influence transcription in a cell-dependent context. One gene can have several transcript versions. Exons are retained regions of a specified processed transcript and can include untranslated sequence; introns are removed by splicing. Coding sequence is the translated part of a coding message. A gene name alone does not specify a transcript, coding interval or protein product.

Preserve the reference sequence, accession and version when describing a variant consequence. DNA sequencing, gene-level RNA counts and protein assays measure different objects; a pooled count does not establish every isoform or an intact active protein. Gene and protein names are often shared, so identify which molecule an assay or drug claim concerns.

In an invented genomic alignment, position V is retained in two transcripts. In A it falls in the coding sequence; in B a later translation start leaves V in an untranslated region. Both can retain the exon containing V. Alignment gaps preserve genomic positions in the drawing, while each processed RNA is continuous. These are two specified transcript models, not measured abundance, an observed variant effect or proof that both messages yield active proteins. Keep their reference accessions and versions with any consequence claim.

Catalysis lowers a reaction’s activation barrier without supplying an unlimited energy source. Most familiar enzymes are proteins, while some RNAs also catalyze reactions. Active-site interactions help chemistry; other binding sites can regulate activity. Binding, catalytic rate, substrate preference and activity in a cell are different properties. An inhibitor can act through the active site or another mechanism, and turnover rates are not one universal number.

For a simple reversible binding equilibrium, Kd is the product of free partner concentrations divided by complex concentration; lower Kd means tighter binding under those conditions. For identical independent sites with one ligand and no competition, fractional occupancy is L / (Kd + L), where L is free ligand concentration. Half occupancy occurs at L = Kd in that model. Total added ligand need not equal free ligand. Affinity for one partner does not establish specificity against other partners.

For a suitable Michaelis-Menten enzyme model, Km is the substrate concentration at half the maximum initial reaction rate. It depends on the catalytic mechanism and conditions and is not generally Kd. Turnover concerns reaction cycling, not binding strength.

IC50 is half inhibition of a specified assay response; EC50 describes half of a defined functional response change. Substrate/ATP concentrations, enzyme or receptor amount, timing and assay design affect these measures. A biochemical inhibition value, a cell-growth value and a clinical outcome are separate evidence.

In a fictional one-site equilibrium example, free ligand and Kd are both 10 nM. With identical independent sites and no competing ligand, occupancy is 10 divided by (10 plus 10), or one half. Five occupied symbols among ten illustrate that model fraction; they are not a guaranteed realised count, a dose recommendation or five dead cells. Binding and release can leave a ligand unchanged. A separate catalytic example changes a substrate bond, retains its atoms in the products and reuses the enzyme. Binding, chemical transformation and a later cellular response therefore need separate measurements.

A full agonist can reach a system’s maximal measured response. A partial agonist has lower activating capacity; its observed maximum depends on receptor amount and amplification and is not defined by giving a smaller dose of a full agonist. Competing partial agonists can reduce a full agonist’s response when they replace it. A neutral antagonist opposes agonist action without changing agonist-independent baseline activity; an inverse agonist reduces that activity when it is measurable. Antagonism need not use the agonist’s binding site.

Kd describes binding under specified conditions. Functional EC50 describes half of the compound’s defined response change in that assay. Measure concentration curves, baseline, a reference agonist, receptor/system context, timing and toxicity controls. Suppressing a signal through toxicity does not prove inverse agonism. Receptor efficacy is not clinical efficacy.

An invented response assay starts at a baseline of 10. Its full agonist tends toward 100, partial agonist toward 40, neutral antagonist stays at 10, and inverse agonist tends toward 5. At one low concentration the full agonist also gives 40; that point does not make it a partial agonist. In a separate condition with a reference agonist present, increasing a neutral antagonist reduces the response from 80 toward 10. Receptor amount, coupling, endpoint, timing and toxicity controls still belong to the comparison; these are chosen response curves, not measured occupancy or clinical effects.

One toy parameterisation uses relative concentration c: full response 10 + 90c/(1+c), partial 10 + 30c/(1+c), neutral 10, and inverse 10 - 5c/(1+c). The full response at c = 0.5 is 40. With the reference agonist fixed, another chosen curve is 10 + 315/(4.5+b), where b is relative antagonist concentration. If these curves are plotted on a log-concentration axis from 0.01 to 1,000, zero is outside the plot; baseline and limiting plateaus need separate statements. The full, partial and inverse curves share c = 1 as the midpoint of their own response changes by construction; this is not evidence of equal measured potency. Different vertical scales also make distances between pictures an unreliable response comparison.

Many protein kinases transfer phosphate from ATP to selected substrate residues, commonly serine, threonine or tyrosine, leaving ADP. Phosphatases remove phosphate through a different reaction, rather than simply making ATP by reversing kinase activity. Kinases can also modify lipids, as PI3K does. Protein amount is distinct from catalytic activity, and not every relay protein is a kinase. In the defined EGFR asymmetric-dimer mechanism, activation-loop phosphorylation was not required for activation.

A simplified branched relay can place a membrane-associated RAS switch, a noncatalytic scaffold holding partners and a kinase in different roles. In the normal RAS switch, the GTP-bound form is active and the GDP-bound form is inactive. These selected roles do not establish one circuit in every tumour. In an invented assay, a site-X phosphorylation signal decreases at 30 minutes while the cell count is unchanged at two days. These are different endpoints at different times. Neither alone establishes direct target engagement, growth dependence or patient benefit, and count icons do not specify how many cells were measured.

Signal transduction uses receptors, second messengers, switches, scaffolds, enzymes and gene regulation in intersecting networks. Not every component is a kinase: RAS is a switch regulated by GTP binding and hydrolysis, and scaffolds organize partners. Kinases can modify proteins or lipids. Responses may involve movement, metabolism, growth, survival or differentiation. The RAS–RAF–MEK–ERK and PI3K–AKT–mTOR systems are examples, rather than a single universal surface-to-nucleus chain.

Time, input, cell type and feedback affect interpretation. An isolated-enzyme assay, one cellular phosphosite and a growth/death outcome measure different properties. Test dependence with suitable functional outcomes and an independent perturbation, controlling exposure, cell entry and unrelated effects.

Receptors can be on the surface or inside a cell. Ligand-gated ion channels regulate ion passage; G-protein-coupled receptors act through G proteins; enzyme-linked receptors can contain an enzyme or recruit a separate one. Intracellular nuclear receptors can regulate transcription with cellular partners. A surface signal can ultimately alter genes, while nuclear-receptor family membership does not fix every molecule permanently in the nucleus or require every effect to use new transcription.

Defined engineered estrogen-receptor experiments detected nuclear and membrane pools; they do not establish a universal proportion in human tumors. Distinguish receptor identity, location, accessible binding and measured function. A positive stain or fluorescence intensity is not automatically a calibrated receptor count, pathway dependence or drug sensitivity.

In a selected cell-edge example, a G-protein-coupled receptor binds a ligand outside the cell and couples to a G protein on the cytoplasmic side. A separate ligand-gated channel has a ligand-binding site and a pore for ions; the chosen open state and inward arrow do not make every binding event open a channel or determine every ion's direction. A hypothetical probe that remains outside can reach an exposed binding site, while a different entering ligand can reach an intracellular receptor and, in a selected route, influence nuclear gene regulation. These are examples of access and relay, not an exhaustive receptor taxonomy or a universal permeability rule. They do not measure receptor abundance, growth dependence or treatment benefit.

Many RTKs have extracellular ligand-binding regions, membrane-spanning regions and intracellular tyrosine-kinase machinery. Families activate differently: Zhang demonstrated an asymmetric EGFR kinase-domain interaction, while Stauber examined an FGF1-FGFR2 extracellular complex with a proposed heparin-related assembly arrangement. Ligand, helper molecules, receptor member and context matter. A downstream phosphosite can have multiple upstream causes and is not a universal receptor meter.

An extracellular EGF ligand can change intracellular kinase signaling without entering the cell. Estrogen and progesterone bind their distinct intracellular receptors, which can regulate transcription with different forms and cellular partners. PD-1 engagement can restrain responding T-cell activity, so receptor activation is not always activation of tumor growth. FAP is a surface protease used as a targeting address, not a hormone/growth-factor receptor in this comparison.

PD-L1 can be on a non-malignant neighbouring cell as well as a tumour cell. In a selected contact example it meets PD-1 on a responding T cell and can restrain that cell's signalling. Other activating and inhibitory inputs remain relevant; a diagram of this interaction does not establish complete shutdown, cell killing or exhaustion. Molecular counts and receptor pairings in the scene are schematic, not a stoichiometry measurement or a treatment-selection test.

Protein kinases commonly transfer phosphate from ATP to a substrate, producing ADP. Protein phosphatases remove phosphate by hydrolysis without regenerating ATP. A modification can affect catalysis, binding, localization or interactions; sites on one protein can have different functions. Src experiments demonstrated an inhibitory tail-phosphorylation mechanism in their defined preparation, so phosphorylation should not be treated as universal activation.

A phosphosite signal depends on modified molecules, parent-protein amount, recovery and measurement. It is not automatically site occupancy, the fraction modified at that site. A parent-normalized ratio may be informative without becoming an absolute occupancy percentage. Retain site identity/localization confidence, method, specimen handling and time.

In a fictional comparison, sample A has a phosphopeptide signal of 1 and a parent-protein signal of 1; sample B has signals of 2 and 2 on the same relative scale. Both ratios are 1, so the doubled phosphopeptide signal alone does not establish an increased modified fraction. Comparable recovery and measurement are assumed; these ratios are neither absolute molecule counts nor calibrated occupancy percentages. In a separate serine-site example, a kinase transfers phosphate from ATP to the site's oxygen and makes ADP. A phosphatase uses water to release phosphate and restore the hydroxyl group, without making ATP. These reactions modify a site on an existing molecule and do not measure how much protein is present.
